prompt:
Which word correctly completes the sentence?

The old bridge was so unsafe that the city closed it ____ instead of fixing it.
spelling_pattern: the compound altogether: al- with a single l, and -gether with e alone (not ea)
error_sites: single l in al-
e alone (no a) in -gether

student_error.alltogether: writes the whole word all at the start, as in the phrase all together
student_error.altogeather: spells the short e sound in -gether as ea, as in feather and weather
student_error.alltogeather: builds the word from all + together and spells the short e as ea, as in weather

explanation: "altogether" is the correct spelling (single l in al-; e alone in -gether). "alltogether" writes the whole word all at the start, as in the phrase all together. "altogeather" spells the short e sound as ea, as in feather and weather. "alltogeather" makes both mistakes.

i between bl and -ity

student_error.possiblity: adds -ty straight onto the bl of possible and leaves out the i, spelling the word as it is said quickly
student_error.posiblity: writes one s and also leaves out the i, spelling the whole word the way it sounds

explanation: "possibility" is the correct spelling (double s as in possible; i between bl and -ity). "posibility" writes one s. "possiblity" leaves out the i after bl. "posiblity" makes both mistakes.

student_error.preformence: writes pre- for per- and -ence for -ance, spelling both unstressed parts by guesswork

student_error.disastrious: adds an i before -ous, as in glorious and industrious

student_error.inexcuseable: keeps the final e of excuse before -able
student_error.innexcuseable: doubles the n and keeps the e of excuse, writing every part in full

choices: After the storm, knocked out the power in our whole neighborhood my brother and I read comic books by flashlight.
After the storm knocked out the power in our whole neighborhood my brother and I read comic books by flashlight.
After the storm knocked out the power in our whole neighborhood, my brother and I read comic books by flashlight.
After the storm, knocked out the power in our whole neighborhood, my brother and I read comic books by flashlight.
correct_answer: After the storm knocked out the power in our whole neighborhood, my brother and I read comic books by flashlight.
error_sites: comma after the whole introductory clause (after neighborhood)
no comma inside the introductory clause (after storm)

student_error.After the storm knocked out the power in: Leaves out the comma after a long introductory clause, so the opening runs into the main sentence.
student_error.After the storm, knocked out the power i: Treats 'After the storm' as a short introductory phrase and puts a comma after it, as well as after the full clause.
Thinks the introductory part is only 'After the storm', so the comma goes after storm instead of after neighborhood.

explanation: The introductory element is the whole clause 'After the storm knocked out the power in our whole neighborhood', so the comma goes after neighborhood. A comma after storm splits the clause's subject (storm) from its verb (knocked).
punct_rule: comma after the full introductory clause, not inside it

choices: Dad packed snacks for the car a map of the state park, and two jackets for the rainy hike.
Dad packed snacks, for the car, a map of the state park, and two jackets for the rainy hike.
Dad packed snacks, for the car a map of the state park, and two jackets for the rainy hike.
Dad packed snacks for the car, a map of the state park, and two jackets for the rainy hike.
correct_answer: Dad packed snacks for the car, a map of the state park, and two jackets for the rainy hike.
error_sites: comma after the whole first phrase in the series (after car)
no comma inside the first phrase (after snacks)

student_error.Dad packed snacks for the car a map of t: Leaves out the comma between the first two phrases in the series.
student_error.Dad packed snacks, for the car, a map of: Puts a comma after every noun, splitting 'snacks' from 'for the car' as well as ending the phrase.
student_error.Dad packed snacks, for the car a map of: Thinks the first item is just 'snacks', so the comma goes after snacks instead of after the whole phrase 'snacks for the car'.

explanation: Each item in the series is a whole phrase: 'snacks for the car', 'a map of the state park', 'two jackets for the rainy hike'. Commas go between the phrases, not inside one, so there is no comma after snacks.
punct_rule: commas between whole phrases in a series, not inside a phrase

choices: You remembered to lock the back door before we left for the airport, didn't you Grandpa?
You remembered to lock the back door before we left for the airport, didn't you, Grandpa.
You remembered to lock the back door before we left for the airport, didn't you, Grandpa?
You remembered to lock the back door before we left for the airport, didn't you Grandpa.
correct_answer: You remembered to lock the back door before we left for the airport, didn't you, Grandpa?
error_sites: comma before the name in direct address at the end
question mark ending the tag question

student_error.You remembered to lock the back door bef: Sets off the tag but forgets that a name at the end, in direct address, also needs a comma before it.
Ends with a period because the sentence starts out as a long statement.
Reads the whole sentence as a statement, so adds no question mark and runs the name onto the tag.

explanation: A name used in direct address is set off with a comma, even at the end of a sentence (', Grandpa'). Because 'didn't you' turns the sentence into a question, it ends with a question mark.
punct_rule: tag question ended with a question mark, with a comma before a name in direct address at the end

choices: Grandpa's old truck, (the blue one parked behind the barn) still starts on the coldest mornings.
Grandpa's old truck (the blue one parked behind the barn) still starts on the coldest mornings.
Grandpa's old truck, (the blue one parked behind the barn), still starts on the coldest mornings.
Grandpa's old truck (the blue one parked behind the barn), still starts on the coldest mornings.
correct_answer: Grandpa's old truck (the blue one parked behind the barn) still starts on the coldest mornings.
error_sites: no comma before the opening parenthesis
no comma after the closing parenthesis

student_error.Grandpa's old truck, (the blue one parke: Adds a comma before the parentheses, where the reader pauses before the added phrase.
student_error.Grandpa's old truck (the blue one parked: Adds a comma after the closing parenthesis, where the reader pauses before the verb.
student_error.Grandpa's old truck, (the blue one parke: Treats the parentheses like commas and sets the phrase off with commas as well, on both sides.

explanation: Parentheses already set off the added phrase, so no comma goes before or after them. Without the parenthetical the sentence is 'Grandpa's old truck still starts on the coldest mornings', with no comma between subject and verb.
punct_rule: parentheses around a nonrestrictive element, with no extra commas around them

choices: By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train has already left and the ticket office had closed for the night.
By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train had already left and the ticket office has closed for the night.
By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train has already left and the ticket office has closed for the night.
By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train had already left and the ticket office had closed for the night.
correct_answer: By the time Grandpa arrived at the station, the last train had already left and the ticket office had closed for the night.
error_sites: 'had already left' (past perfect) for the first action finished before Grandpa arrived
'had closed' (past perfect) for the second action finished before Grandpa arrived

student_error.By the time Grandpa arrived at the stati: Uses present perfect 'has left' for an action that was finished before another past action.
Gets the first verb right but slips into present perfect 'has closed' for the second earlier action.
Uses present perfect 'has' for both earlier actions, not knowing that a past event needs 'had'.

explanation: The sentence is set in the past (arrived). Both the train leaving and the office closing happened before Grandpa arrived, so both need the past perfect: 'had already left' and 'had closed'. Present perfect 'has' does not fit an action completed before another past action.
varied_dimension: past perfect vs present perfect, first verb; past perfect vs present perfect, second verb

choices: My cousin, he has never seen the ocean, is visiting us next week, and we are taking him to the beach on Saturday.
My cousin, who has never seen the ocean, is visiting us next week, we are taking him to the beach on Saturday.
My cousin, he has never seen the ocean, is visiting us next week, we are taking him to the beach on Saturday.
My cousin, who has never seen the ocean, is visiting us next week, and we are taking him to the beach on Saturday.
correct_answer: My cousin, who has never seen the ocean, is visiting us next week, and we are taking him to the beach on Saturday.
error_sites: relative pronoun 'who' introducing the dependent clause inside the sentence
'and' joining the two independent clauses

student_error.My cousin, he has never seen the ocean,: Writes 'he' as in speech, wedging a complete sentence inside another instead of a 'who' clause.
student_error.My cousin, who has never seen the ocean,: Joins two complete sentences with only a comma.
student_error.My cousin, he has never seen the ocean,: Strings complete thoughts together with commas, the way they are spoken, without 'who' or 'and' to connect them.

explanation: The added information about the cousin must be a dependent clause beginning with 'who'; 'he has never seen the ocean' is a complete sentence and cannot sit inside another one. The two independent clauses must be joined by a comma and a conjunction such as 'and', or the result is a comma splice.
varied_dimension: relative clause vs a wedged-in independent clause; missing coordinating conjunction (comma splice)

choices: The gym floor is being repaired and the bleachers are been painted, so the spring dance has been moved to the cafeteria.
The gym floor is been repaired and the bleachers are been painted, so the spring dance has been moved to the cafeteria.
The gym floor is been repaired and the bleachers are being painted, so the spring dance has been moved to the cafeteria.
The gym floor is being repaired and the bleachers are being painted, so the spring dance has been moved to the cafeteria.
correct_answer: The gym floor is being repaired and the bleachers are being painted, so the spring dance has been moved to the cafeteria.
error_sites: progressive passive helper 'is being'
progressive passive helper 'are being'

student_error.The gym floor is been repaired and the b: Uses 'been' after every form of 'be', not knowing that 'been' only follows has, have or had.

explanation: The progressive passive is a form of 'be' (is, are) + 'being' + the past participle: 'is being repaired', 'are being painted'. 'Been' follows has, have or had, as in 'has been moved'.
varied_dimension: progressive passive with 'is' (is being); progressive passive with 'are' (are being), set against the perfect passive 'has been'
